reference.source: Williams Obstetrics / RCOG and international gestational trophoblastic disease guidance
clinicalPearls: Classically presents with irregular vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy, a uterus large for dates, and markedly raised beta-hCG
A complete mole is typically diploid and androgenetic (usually 46,XX from a single sperm duplicating in an empty ovum) with no identifiable foetal tissue
A partial mole is usually triploid (extra paternal chromosome set) and may contain abnormal foetal or embryonic tissue
Pelvic ultrasound may show the classic 'snowstorm' or cluster-of-grapes appearance with theca-lutein cysts of the ovaries
Early excessive beta-hCG can provoke hyperemesis, early pre-eclampsia, and hyperthyroid features from cross-reactivity at the TSH receptor
Definitive management is suction evacuation of the uterus followed by serial beta-hCG surveillance to detect persistent disease
Registration with a trophoblastic disease service and reliable contraception during follow-up are important so rising hCG is not confused with a new pregnancy
Complete moles carry a higher risk of progressing to gestational trophoblastic neoplasia than partial moles
reference.pathophysiology: Hydatidiform mole is an abnormal pregnancy arising from aberrant fertilisation with an excess of paternal genetic material, producing hydropic swelling of chorionic villi and trophoblastic proliferation. In a complete mole an ovum lacking functional maternal genetic material is fertilised and the paternal genome is duplicated (or two sperm enter), giving diploid androgenetic tissue with no viable foetus. In a partial mole a normal ovum is fertilised by two sperm (or a diploid sperm), giving a triploid conceptus with some foetal tissue and focal villous change. Exuberant trophoblast secretes high levels of beta-hCG, and the abnormal trophoblast retains malignant potential, so a proportion of cases progress to invasive or metastatic trophoblastic neoplasia after evacuation.
additionalDifferentials: Choriocarcinoma or other gestational trophoblastic neoplasia
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative serum beta-hCG with serial monitoring
Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound for molar features and theca-lutein cysts
Histopathological examination and ploidy analysis of evacuated tissue
Full blood count and blood group with antibody screen
Thyroid function and pre-eclampsia screening when clinically indicated
Chest imaging if trophoblastic neoplasia or metastasis is suspected
redFlags: Heavy or ongoing vaginal haemorrhage with haemodynamic compromise
Signs of early severe pre-eclampsia before the usual gestation
Features of thyroid storm from very high beta-hCG
Respiratory distress suggesting trophoblastic pulmonary embolisation
Beta-hCG that plateaus or rises after evacuation, indicating persistent neoplasia
reference.prognosis: With timely evacuation and structured beta-hCG surveillance, most molar pregnancies resolve completely and future fertility is usually preserved. A minority progress to gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, which is highly curable when detected early through follow-up.
pitfalls: Attributing early heavy bleeding or hyperemesis simply to a normal or failing pregnancy and missing molar features
Failing to enrol the patient in structured beta-hCG follow-up after evacuation
Allowing a new pregnancy during surveillance so that rising hCG masks persistent disease
Assuming a partial mole has no malignant potential and abandoning monitoring prematurely
references: RCOG guidance on gestational trophoblastic disease
management: Suction evacuation of the uterus is the definitive treatment, with oxytocic use minimised until evacuation is under way
Anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis for rhesus-negative women
Registration with a trophoblastic disease centre and structured serial beta-hCG surveillance to detect persistent or malignant trophoblastic disease
Reliable contraception with avoidance of pregnancy until beta-hCG has normalised and follow-up is complete
Chemotherapy, for example methotrexate for low-risk disease, if gestational trophoblastic neoplasia develops
Management of associated hyperthyroidism, early pre-eclampsia, and hyperemesis around the time of evacuation
Histopathological and ploidy examination of evacuated tissue to confirm complete versus partial mole
